items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Bill Finnegan, Eddie Bert, people that you interviewed that I watched the interviews and listened.

ctx.x: performing headliners, one was Sarah Vaughan and one was Steve Allen. Yeah. I said wow. And it was a two week festival. And it wasn’t just performances. It was workshops that you could attend. And these workshops were from square dancing to photography to charcoal drawing to classical violin, singing, dancing, you name it. Arts festival. And they had to two week cabaret class. Not my thing but the instructor was a woman by the name of Chris Calloway. Cab’s daughter. Well that was enough for me to sign up. Cab…

people who really could play, as opposed to people who couldn’t play that good. That’s who I was usually playing with. And it felt good. And I thought you know I’m getting kind of tired of bouncing around on a piece of equipment, maybe I’ll go back to the East Coast. I’ll go to New York City and I’ll see if I can make a little noise. Because these people encouraged me. And in my mind, and I’ve said this to a few people and I’m going to say it again although I don’t have rehearsed lines, but I knew that — I went…
Did you have your grub stake to see you through for a while?

items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I’ve been really fortunate in being around some musicians that I was buying their LPs when I was a kid. Eddie Bert said to me, “you know why we swing?

ctx.x: I think metronomes are really important. Most singers hate them. Most musicians don’t like them because they’ve got this ugly click-click. But that’s — I tell them, I explain to them I say, “a long time ago metronomes were these big clumsy things that you’d wind up. Then they made them so you could plug them in the wall. Now they make them really small. So buy the smallest one you can, put fresh batteries in it, and swallow it. That way

you’ll always have good time.” Because time is what makes it happen. I mean I don’t want to hear somebody out of tune, but I’d rather hear them out of tune than out of time. Because if you’re in time at least there’s a groove. I mean I don’t want to hear out of tune either, but time, to me — I’ve been really fortunate in being around some musicians that I was buying their LPs when I was a kid. Eddie Bert said to me, “you know why we swing? Because we used to play for dancers. And we know how to swing. Because if…
Yeah. Even if they can’t. Even if there’s no room they can feel it.
